text: Plain gradient boosting works, but production projects need more: regularization against overfitting, native handling of missing values, speed on large tables, and a way to stop training automatically. XGBoost, eXtreme Gradient Boosting, adds all of that, and it's been a staple of tabular competitions and production models for years.

XGBoost adds regularization through reg_lambda, reg_alpha, and gamma; fits trees using both the gradient and second derivative of the loss for better splits; learns which direction missing values should go at every split, so you can pass NaN without imputing; and subsamples rows and columns like a random forest.

On a synthetic six thousand row churn table, we split three ways: train, validation, and test. The validation set lets early stopping watch performance during training, while the test set stays untouched until the very end. That gives three thousand six hundred rows to fit, nine hundred to validate, and fifteen hundred for the final score.

We ask XGBClassifier for up to five hundred trees, but set early_stopping_rounds to thirty, so training stops once validation A.U.C. hasn't improved in thirty rounds. On this data it ran a hundred forty-seven rounds and kept round one sixteen as the best, with validation A.U.C. of zero point eight five one.

The results: logistic regression scores zero point eight zero five test A.U.C.; XGBoost with early stopping scores zero point eight two eight; training all five hundred trees with no stopping scores zero point eight one nine. Stopping at the right round beat both the linear baseline and the un-stopped model.

Feature importances come out roughly: days_since_order zero point three six, tenure_months zero point three two, support_calls zero point one two, plan zero point one two, monthly_spend zero point zero nine. These describe how much the trees used each feature, not causal effect -- treat them as a starting point, not a verdict.

XGBoost is gradient boosting with regularization, missing-value handling, and speed. Use a validation set with early_stopping_rounds so the data chooses the number of trees. Next, we meet two alternatives, LightGBM and CatBoost, and see when each is the better tool.
